carry out hygiene practises in sleeping areas for a healthy environment
advocate for the importance of observing hygiene in sleeping areas

skills.name: Identify locally available things used as bedding and say how to keep a sleeping area clean
skills.mastery: Names locally available bedding (mattress, mat, blanket, bedsheet, pillow, sisal or reed mat, gunny-bag mattress) and says how a sleeping area is kept clean: air and sun the bedding, wash sheets, sweep under the bed, keep food and shoes away, wash and air bedding after bedwetting without shaming. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) carry out hygiene practises in sleeping areas for a healthy environment.
question_forms: what to do to keep bedding clean

prerequisites.reason: Personal and common items at home: bedding is a personal item. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Materials for cleaning personal items are used again for bedding. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Cleaning materials for a home come before cleaning a sleeping area. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only a bought mattress counts as bedding, not a mat, reeds or a gunny-bag mattress.

example.question: Which of these can be used as bedding? A sisal mat, a cooking pot, a spoon.
example.wrong_answer: None of them, bedding is a mattress
example.correct_answer: A sisal mat

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen bedding sold in shops and links the word only with a mattress.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "None of them, bedding is a mattress" beside "A sisal mat" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a mat, a blanket and a gunny-bag mattress. Ask: can you sleep on it or under it? Then it is bedding.
misconceptions.feedback: Bedding is anything we sleep on or under. A mat or a blanket is bedding too.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks bedding that looks clean never needs washing or airing.

example.question: Wanjiru's blanket looks clean. Should she still put it in the sun sometimes?
example.correct_answer: Yes, sun and air kill germs and remove smells

misconceptions.cause: Children judge clean by what they can see; germs and sweat cannot be seen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, it looks clean" beside "Yes, sun and air kill germs and remove smells" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Smell a blanket aired in the sun and one kept folded for weeks. Say: germs hide where we cannot see.
misconceptions.feedback: Bedding can look clean and still have germs. Air it in the sun and wash it often.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks eating on the bed is fine as long as the crumbs are shaken off.

example.question: Where should we eat our food?
example.wrong_answer: On the bed, then shake it
example.correct_answer: At the table or on a mat, away from the bed

misconceptions.cause: Eating in bed is common at home and nothing bad seems to follow at once.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "On the bed, then shake it" beside "At the table or on a mat, away from the bed" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show how crumbs bring ants, cockroaches and rats. Agree: food stays away from where we sleep.
misconceptions.feedback: Crumbs on the bed bring ants and rats. We eat away from our sleeping place.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks wet bedding after bedwetting should be folded and hidden so nobody knows.

example.question: A child wets the bed at night. What should be done with the wet bedding?
example.correct_answer: Wash it or put it in the sun to dry, and the child washes

misconceptions.cause: The child fears shame, so hiding feels safest.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Fold it and hide it" beside "Wash it or put it in the sun to dry, and the child washes" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say calmly that many children wet the bed. Wet bedding is washed and dried in the sun; the child bathes. No one is laughed at.
misconceptions.feedback: Wet bedding is washed and dried in the sun. Many children wet the bed. It is nothing to hide or laugh at.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy: learner identifies and talks about the need for help when role-playing expressions of emotional needs.
sub_strands.values: Love: learner portrays a caring attitude when comforting others who are hurting.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills: learner identifies how to cope with emotions expressed by self and others.
sub_strands.links: Emotional needs in a family draws skills of compassion, empathy, love, and kindness aspects in Religious Activities. Feeling words used in songs and stories involving emotions relates to vocabulary learnt in English Language Activities.

outcomes.text: describe how people express feelings in real-life

label emotions expressed by self and others

skills.name: Label emotions in self and others and describe how people express them
skills.mastery: Labels happy, sad, angry, afraid and surprised in faces, body and stories, describes how people show them (smiling, laughing, crying, frowning, shouting, shaking, hiding), knows a person can cry for joy and that boys and girls both have all feelings. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: picture of a face: which feeling
what a person does when feeling it

prerequisites.reason: Needs and wants come before the emotional needs of a family. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Basic needs of a family, which emotional needs add to. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

skills.name: Describe ways in which emotional needs are met in real-life situations
skills.mastery: Says that people need love, care, comfort, praise, being listened to and feeling safe, and describes how they are met: a hug, kind words, listening, playing together, praising good work, comforting someone who is sad; knows money and gifts alone do not meet them. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which action meets an emotional need

prerequisites.reason: Naming a feeling comes before knowing what the person needs. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Sorting needs from wants comes before naming emotional needs. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks boys do not feel sad or cry, so a crying boy is weak.

example.question: Otieno falls and cries. What is he feeling?
example.correct_answer: Pain or sadness: boys feel sad and cry too

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard "boys don't cry" at home or in play.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, boys do not cry" beside "Pain or sadness: boys feel sad and cry too" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Read a story where a father cries at good news. Say: everyone has feelings, boys and girls.
misconceptions.feedback: Boys and girls both feel sad and both may cry. Crying is a way of showing a feeling.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks tears always mean sadness.

example.question: Grandmother cries when her son comes home after many years. How does she feel?
example.correct_answer: Happy (tears of joy)

misconceptions.cause: Most tears the child has seen came with sadness or pain.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sad" beside "Happy (tears of joy)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a picture of a happy reunion with tears. Ask what made her cry, then name joy.
misconceptions.feedback: People can cry when they are very happy too. Look at what is happening to know the feeling.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks feeling angry makes someone a bad person.

example.question: Achieng feels angry when her book is torn. Is Achieng a bad girl?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, she is angry so she is bad
example.correct_answer: No, feeling angry is normal; what matters is what she does next

misconceptions.cause: Children are often punished when angry, so the feeling itself seems wrong.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, she is angry so she is bad" beside "No, feeling angry is normal; what matters is what she does next" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Separate the feeling from the action: angry is fine, hitting is not. Practise calm steps: breathe, tell an adult.
misconceptions.feedback: Feeling angry is normal. We choose what to do: breathe, then talk to an adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Looks only at the mouth to name a feeling, so a forced smile or a frightened face with an open mouth is misread.

example.question: A child stands shaking with wide eyes and an open mouth while a dog barks. How does she feel?
example.correct_answer: Afraid

misconceptions.cause: Young children first learn feelings from smiley and sad mouth drawings.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Happy, her mouth is open" beside "Afraid" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Look at eyes, hands and body as well as the mouth. Act out afraid with the whole body.
misconceptions.feedback: Look at the eyes and the body too. Shaking and wide eyes show fear.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks giving things (sweets, money, toys) is the way to meet every emotional need.

example.question: Baraka is sad because his grandfather is sick. What will help him most?
example.correct_answer: Sit with him, listen and comfort him

misconceptions.cause: Children see gifts given at happy times and think gifts fix feelings.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Give him sweets" beside "Sit with him, listen and comfort him" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Role-play two ways to help a sad friend: a sweet and walking away, or listening. Ask which felt better.
misconceptions.feedback: A sad friend needs someone to listen and comfort them. Kind words and care help more than gifts.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks needs are only food, clothes and shelter, so love is not a need.

example.question: Is love a need?
example.wrong_answer: No, only food, clothes and a house are needs
example.correct_answer: Yes, love and care are emotional needs

misconceptions.cause: Grade 1 and 2 taught basic needs as things you can touch.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only food, clothes and a house are needs" beside "Yes, love and care are emotional needs" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Add a fourth column to the needs chart: love, care, praise. Say: we need these to grow well inside.
misconceptions.feedback: Love and care are needs too. They help us feel safe and happy.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only small babies need comfort and care, not big children or adults.

example.question: Mother is tired and sad after a long day. What can a child do?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, adults do not need comfort
example.correct_answer: Greet her kindly, help her and give her a hug

misconceptions.cause: The child sees comfort given mostly to babies.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, adults do not need comfort" beside "Greet her kindly, help her and give her a hug" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Tell a story of a child who comforts a parent. Everyone needs love, at every age.
misconceptions.feedback: Everyone needs love and care, even grown-ups. You can help with kind words and help.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks praising someone makes them proud, so good work should not be praised.

example.question: Akinyi sweeps the class well. What should the teacher say?
example.correct_answer: Well done, thank you

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard adults warn against "spoiling" children.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, praise makes her proud" beside "Well done, thank you" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show how praise makes a classmate want to help again. Praise the action, kindly.
misconceptions.feedback: Saying "well done" helps people feel valued. It meets a need.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: share ideas on different food items found in the locality,
use digital devices or print media to search for information on various food groups,
use pictures of common food items or video clips to classify various food items,
use digital devices or print media to search for information on table manners,
role play good table manners when taking meals,
observe good table manners when taking meals,
share reasons why people eat too much or too little food,
use video clips, print media, or age-appropriate case stories to find out what happens when a person eats too much or too little food.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we have different food items in the locality?
What activities do you engage in while eating?
sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy: learner develops self-awareness when finding out what happens when a person eats too much or too little food.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: learner enhances self-drive while observing good table manners when taking meals.
sub_strands.pcis: Health promotion issues: learner advocates for eating the right amount of food to prevent non-communicable diseases.
sub_strands.links: Grouping food items relates to skills of sorting and grouping learnt in Mathematical Activities.

outcomes.text: identify common food items found in the immediate environment
classify food items into three food groups
observe table manners during meals
embrace good eating habits to promote good health

skills.name: Identify common food items found locally and classify them into the three food groups
skills.mastery: Names common local foods and puts them in the three food groups: energy-giving (ugali, rice, potatoes, cassava, bread, bananas for cooking), body-building (beans, meat, eggs, fish, milk, omena, ndengu) and protective (fruits and vegetables: sukuma wiki, cabbage, mangoes, oranges, carrots); knows a balanced meal has all three. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) observe table manners during meals.
question_forms: which group a food belongs to

prerequisites.reason: Food items from animals: most are body-building foods. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Food from plants and animals comes before the three food groups. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Sorting fruits and vegetables: the protective group. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts ugali in the body-building group because it makes one strong and full.

example.question: Which group does ugali belong to?
example.correct_answer: Energy-giving

misconceptions.cause: Adults say "eat ugali to grow strong", and the child links strong with body-building.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Body-building" beside "Energy-giving" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say: ugali gives energy to run and play. Beans and eggs build the body. Sort a plate of ugali, beans and sukuma.
misconceptions.feedback: Ugali gives us energy to work and play. It is an energy-giving food.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks protective foods are only sweet fruits, so vegetables like sukuma wiki are not protective.

example.question: Is sukuma wiki a protective food?
example.wrong_answer: No, protective foods are sweet fruits
example.correct_answer: Yes, vegetables and fruits are protective foods

misconceptions.cause: Fruits are taught as healthy treats; greens are eaten as a side dish.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, protective foods are sweet fruits" beside "Yes, vegetables and fruits are protective foods" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Put sukuma, cabbage, mango and orange in one basket labelled protective. Say: they help us fight disease.
misconceptions.feedback: Vegetables like sukuma wiki and fruits both protect our bodies from disease.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks milk is a drink, not a food, so it has no food group.

example.question: Which group does milk belong to?
example.wrong_answer: None, milk is only a drink
example.correct_answer: Body-building

misconceptions.cause: Milk is poured into a cup like water or tea.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "None, milk is only a drink" beside "Body-building" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show that milk comes from a cow like meat and helps babies grow. It is a body-building food.
misconceptions.feedback: Milk is a body-building food. It helps our bones and body grow.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a full plate of one food (a big plate of rice) is a good meal.

example.question: Which meal is balanced? A: rice only. B: rice, beans and cabbage.
example.correct_answer: B, it has all three food groups

misconceptions.cause: Being full is the child's sign of a good meal.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A, it fills you" beside "B, it has all three food groups" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Draw a plate in three parts. Fill each part with one group. Say: a good meal has all three.
misconceptions.feedback: A good meal has energy food, body-building food and protective food together.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.mastery: Sorts places into safe (home, school, church or mosque, a police station, a hospital, a playground with adults) and unsafe (quarries, deep pits, open wells, rivers and dams, busy roads, dumping sites, abandoned buildings, near fallen electric wires), and names ways to keep safe: walk in groups, go straight home, do not go with or take gifts from strangers, keep away from fallen wires, tell a trusted adult. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

what to do if a stranger offers a gift

Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what to do at the sign

Safety on the way to school, where roads are crossed. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a stranger who is kind or offers sweets is safe to go with.

example.question: A kind stranger offers you sweets and a ride home. What should you do?
example.wrong_answer: Go with him, he is kind
example.correct_answer: Say no, walk away and tell a trusted adult

misconceptions.cause: Children judge people by how nice they seem.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Go with him, he is kind" beside "Say no, walk away and tell a trusted adult" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Role-play saying "No, thank you" and walking to a trusted adult. Kind words do not make a stranger safe.
misconceptions.feedback: Never go with a stranger or take gifts, even if they are kind. Say no and tell a trusted adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a river or dam is a safe place to play if you can stand in it.

example.question: Is a dam a safe place to play without an adult?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, if the water is not deep
example.correct_answer: No, it is unsafe: water can be deep and you can drown

misconceptions.cause: The edge looks shallow and the child cannot see the deep part.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, if the water is not deep" beside "No, it is unsafe: water can be deep and you can drown" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a picture of a dam with a hidden deep middle. Rule: no water play without an adult.
misconceptions.feedback: Rivers and dams are unsafe without an adult. The water can be deeper than it looks.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a fallen electric wire is safe to touch or play with if it is not sparking.

example.question: You see a wire lying on the ground after a storm. What should you do?
example.wrong_answer: Pick it up and move it
example.correct_answer: Keep far away and tell an adult

misconceptions.cause: A wire looks like a rope; the danger cannot be seen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Pick it up and move it" beside "Keep far away and tell an adult" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say: a fallen wire can kill even when quiet. Stay far, tell an adult to call Kenya Power.
misconceptions.feedback: Never touch a fallen wire. Keep far away and tell an adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks danger only comes from strangers, so any known person can ask them to keep secrets.

example.question: A neighbour asks you to keep a secret touch from your parents. What should you do?
example.wrong_answer: Keep the secret, he is not a stranger
example.correct_answer: Tell a trusted adult at once

misconceptions.cause: Children are told only "beware of strangers".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Keep the secret, he is not a stranger" beside "Tell a trusted adult at once" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Teach the rule: no secret about touching, from anyone. Name trusted adults at home and school.
misconceptions.feedback: If anyone, even someone you know, asks you to keep a secret about touching, tell a trusted adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a zebra crossing means cars will always stop, so you can cross without looking.

example.question: You reach a zebra crossing. What do you do?
example.wrong_answer: Cross at once, cars must stop
example.correct_answer: Stop, look right, left and right again, and cross when cars have stopped

misconceptions.cause: The child is told the crossing is "for people" and thinks it protects by itself.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Cross at once, cars must stop" beside "Stop, look right, left and right again, and cross when cars have stopped" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Practise at a chalk crossing: stop, look, wait for cars to stop, then walk.
misconceptions.feedback: At a zebra crossing, stop and look both ways. Cross only when the cars have stopped.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the green traffic light for cars means people may cross.

example.question: The traffic light for cars is green. Can you cross?
example.correct_answer: No, green means cars go; wait

misconceptions.cause: Green means go in every game the child knows.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, green means go" beside "No, green means cars go; wait" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show both lights: green for cars means cars move. People cross when the walking figure is green.
misconceptions.feedback: When the light for cars is green, cars move. Wait until it is safe to cross.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Looks only one way before crossing.

example.question: Before crossing a road in Kenya, which way do you look first?
example.correct_answer: Right, then left, then right again

misconceptions.cause: The child copies others who glance once.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only left" beside "Right, then left, then right again" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Practise "right, left, right" aloud at a chalk road. In Kenya cars drive on the left, so the near cars come from the right.
misconceptions.feedback: Look right, then left, then right again before you cross.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the stop sign tells people walking to stop and never cross.

example.question: Who must stop at a stop sign?
example.correct_answer: Drivers (and everyone must take care)

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the word stop and takes it as an order for himself.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a cultural event is only a party with music and food.

example.question: Is a tree-planting ceremony a cultural event?
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is an event the community does together

misconceptions.cause: Events the child has seen were celebrations with food.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, there is no party" beside "Yes, it is an event the community does together" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: List events with and without parties. Say: a cultural event is what a community does together by its ways.
misconceptions.feedback: A cultural event is something a community does together, like planting trees or a wedding.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks cultural events have nothing to do with caring for the environment.

example.question: Which event cares for the environment?
example.correct_answer: A tree-planting ceremony (a clean-up day)

misconceptions.cause: Caring for the environment is taught in science lessons, not with culture.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A wedding, because people dance" beside "A tree-planting ceremony (a clean-up day)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show pictures of a tree planted at a naming or a clean-up after a harvest feast. Sort them.
misconceptions.feedback: Some cultural events care for the environment, like planting trees together.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an event can only do one thing, so it is either social or environmental.

example.question: A school cultural day ends with everyone planting trees. What does it do?
example.correct_answer: Both: brings people together and cares for the environment

misconceptions.cause: Sorting into two boxes makes the child think each item fits only one.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only brings people together" beside "Both: brings people together and cares for the environment" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Use a Venn diagram: social well-being, environmental care, both in the middle.
misconceptions.feedback: One event can bring people together and care for the environment at the same time.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks other communities' events are strange or wrong because they differ from his own.

example.question: A classmate's community has a different naming ceremony. What should we think?
example.wrong_answer: It is wrong because it is not like ours
example.correct_answer: It is their way; we can learn about it and respect it

misconceptions.cause: Children see their own ways as the normal ones.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is wrong because it is not like ours" beside "It is their way; we can learn about it and respect it" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Invite children to share events from their communities. Find what all of them have in common: bringing people together.
misconceptions.feedback: Different communities have different events. We learn about them and respect them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Describe unfavourable weather conditions, explain their dangers and say how to respond safely
skills.mastery: Describes unfavourable weather (very hot and dry, heavy rain and floods, strong winds, thunder and lightning, hailstones, very cold) and explains its dangers to people (drowning, being struck by lightning, sunburn and thirst, falling trees and roofs, colds and chest illness), and says the safe response: stay indoors in lightning, never shelter under a tall tree, never cross a flooded river, drink water and wear a hat in heat, wear warm clothes in cold. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the weather in the picture

prerequisites.reason: Naming weather conditions comes before knowing which are dangerous. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Predicting weather helps a child prepare for bad weather. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a tall tree is the best shelter in a thunderstorm.

example.question: It starts to thunder and rain while you walk home. Where do you go?
example.correct_answer: Into a building, away from tall trees

misconceptions.cause: A tree keeps you dry from rain, so it seems safe in any storm.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Under the tallest tree" beside "Into a building, away from tall trees" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show that lightning strikes the tallest thing. Practise going into a building or crouching low in the open.
misconceptions.feedback: In lightning, never shelter under a tall tree. Go into a building.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks moving floodwater is safe to cross if it only reaches the knees.

example.question: A small river is flooded up to your knees on the way to school. What do you do?
example.correct_answer: Do not cross; go back or wait for an adult

misconceptions.cause: The water looks shallow and the child cannot see its force.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Walk across quickly" beside "Do not cross; go back or wait for an adult" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show how a little moving water can push over a child. Rule: turn back, wait for an adult.
misconceptions.feedback: Never cross a flooded river, even if it looks shallow. Wait for an adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks hot sunny weather can never be unfavourable because sunshine is good.

example.question: Can very hot weather be dangerous?
example.correct_answer: Yes, it can cause thirst, sunburn and drought

misconceptions.cause: Sunny is called "good weather" in songs and greetings.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, sunshine is always good" beside "Yes, it can cause thirst, sunburn and drought" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Talk about a drought: dry rivers, dying crops and thirst. Name the safe actions: water, shade, hat.
misconceptions.feedback: Very hot weather can be dangerous. Drink water, stay in the shade and cover your head.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks lightning is only dangerous when it is raining hard, so playing outside during distant thunder is fine.

example.question: You hear thunder but it is not raining yet. Can you keep playing football in the field?
example.correct_answer: No, go indoors when you hear thunder

misconceptions.cause: The child links danger with rain, which can be felt, not with thunder.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, until the rain comes" beside "No, go indoors when you hear thunder" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Teach the rule: when thunder roars, go indoors. Lightning can strike before the rain.
misconceptions.feedback: When you hear thunder, go indoors. Lightning can strike before the rain.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: List the characteristics of different types of soil and say how soil is conserved
skills.mastery: Lists characteristics of sand (rough, loose, big particles, light colour, water drains through fast), clay (smooth, sticky when wet, tiny particles, holds water, cracks when dry) and loam (dark, crumbly, a mixture, good for plants), and names soil conservation activities: mulching, manuring, planting trees and grass, and not leaving soil bare. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. prerequisites.reason: Classifying soils in Grade 2 comes before listing their characteristics. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Types of soil found in the locality. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks all soil is the same and differs only in colour.

example.question: Is sand the same as clay soil?
example.correct_answer: No, sand is rough and loose, clay is smooth and sticky

misconceptions.cause: Soil looks like one brown material from a distance.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, soil is soil" beside "No, sand is rough and loose, clay is smooth and sticky" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Let the child rub sand and clay between the fingers and roll each wet. Name the feel.
misconceptions.feedback: Soils are different. Sand is rough and loose, clay is smooth and sticky.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks water drains fastest through clay because it is soft.

example.question: Water is poured on sand and on clay. Which lets water through faster?
example.correct_answer: Sand

misconceptions.cause: Soft things seem to soak and let through more.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Clay" beside "Sand" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Pour water through sand and clay in two bottles with holes. Count how fast it drips.
misconceptions.feedback: Water passes through sand quickly. Clay holds water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sand is the best soil for plants because it is clean.

example.question: Which soil is best for growing vegetables?
example.correct_answer: Loam

misconceptions.cause: Sand looks clean and nice, so it seems good.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sand" beside "Loam" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Grow beans in sand, clay and loam pots. Watch which grows best. Name loam.
misconceptions.feedback: Loam is best for most plants. It is dark and holds water and food for plants.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks bare, swept soil is good for the environment and mulch is just rubbish.

example.question: Which garden protects the soil better: bare soil or soil covered with dry grass?

misconceptions.cause: Children sweep compounds bare, so bare looks tidy and right.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Bare soil, it is clean" beside "Soil covered with dry grass (mulch)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Pour water on a bare tray and a mulched tray of soil. See which washes away.
misconceptions.feedback: Covering soil with dry grass (mulch) stops it from washing away and keeps it wet.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: List sources of heat in the environment and identify their uses
skills.mastery: Lists sources of heat (the sun, fire from firewood or charcoal, a gas or paraffin stove, electricity in a cooker, iron or kettle, the body) and identifies uses (cooking, warming the body and house, drying clothes and grain, ironing, boiling water), and knows ways to save heat: cover the pot, use an energy-saving jiko, put out the fire after cooking. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. misconceptions.error: Thinks everything that gives light gives heat, so a torch or a phone screen is a heat source.

example.question: Which is a source of heat: a torch or a charcoal jiko?
example.correct_answer: The charcoal jiko

misconceptions.cause: Light and heat came together in the sun and fire the child knows.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The torch" beside "The charcoal jiko" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Hold a hand near a torch and near a warm jiko (safely). Feel which is warm.
misconceptions.feedback: Some things give light but little heat, like a torch. A jiko gives heat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the sun gives only light, not heat.

example.question: Why do clothes dry when hung in the sun?
example.correct_answer: The sun gives heat that dries them

misconceptions.cause: The sun is taught first as giving day and light.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Because of the wind only" beside "The sun gives heat that dries them" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Put two wet cloths, one in sun and one in shade. Feel and compare after an hour.
misconceptions.feedback: The sun gives heat as well as light. Its heat dries clothes and grain.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks covering a cooking pot does not matter for saving heat.

example.question: Which pot of water boils faster: covered or uncovered?
example.wrong_answer: Uncovered, so we can see it
example.correct_answer: Covered, the lid keeps the heat in

misconceptions.cause: An open pot lets the cook watch, so it seems better.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Uncovered, so we can see it" beside "Covered, the lid keeps the heat in" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Boil two small pots, one covered. Time them. Say: the lid keeps heat in and saves fuel.
misconceptions.feedback: A lid keeps heat in the pot. Food cooks faster and we use less firewood.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a fire can be left burning after cooking because it will go out by itself.

example.question: Cooking is finished. What should be done with the fire?
example.wrong_answer: Leave it, it will go out
example.correct_answer: Put it out safely to save fuel and prevent burns

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen fires die down slowly on their own.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Leave it, it will go out" beside "Put it out safely to save fuel and prevent burns" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show how embers can flare up and burn. An adult puts out the fire; children keep away.
misconceptions.feedback: After cooking, the fire is put out by an adult. This saves fuel and stops burns.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

example.question: Water has gone through a sand and cloth filter. What else should be done before drinking?
example.correct_answer: Boil it

misconceptions.cause: The filtered water looks clean, so the job seems done.

misconceptions.help: Filter muddy water: it looks clear. Say: the filter removes dirt, boiling kills germs.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.cause: Children explore by tasting, and many berries look like fruit.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Taste one to check" beside "Do not taste; ask an adult first" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show pictures of a safe and a poisonous berry that look alike. Rule: never taste, ask an adult.
misconceptions.feedback: Never taste an unknown berry or plant. Ask an adult first.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks brightly coloured or nice-smelling plants are safe to eat.

example.question: A flower smells sweet. Is it safe to eat?
example.correct_answer: Not unless an adult says it is food

misconceptions.cause: Sweet smells and bright colours are linked with sweets and fruit.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it smells nice" beside "Not unless an adult says it is food" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Name a pretty but poisonous plant grown near homes. Looks and smell do not tell us.
misconceptions.feedback: A plant can look or smell nice and still be poisonous. Ask an adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks stinging nettle or thorny plants can be pulled with bare hands if done quickly.

example.question: You need to pull out stinging nettle in the garden. What do you use?
example.correct_answer: Gloves, a cloth or a tool

misconceptions.cause: Speed seems to protect, as when touching something hot.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Bare hands, quickly" beside "Gloves, a cloth or a tool" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show gloves and a jembe. Practise pulling weeds with gloves only.
misconceptions.feedback: Use gloves or a tool to handle stinging or thorny plants.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks hands do not need washing after handling plants because plants are clean.

example.question: You have weeded the garden. What do you do before eating?
example.correct_answer: Wash hands with soap and water

misconceptions.cause: Plants seem natural and clean, unlike toilets.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Eat, plants are clean" beside "Wash hands with soap and water" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show the soil and sap left on hands. Some plants can irritate eyes and mouths.
misconceptions.feedback: Wash your hands after handling plants and soil.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks that a plant animals eat (grass) is edible for people.

example.question: Cows eat grass. Is grass edible for people?
example.correct_answer: No, grass is not food for people

misconceptions.cause: The child reasons that food for one is food for all.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, cows eat it" beside "No, grass is not food for people" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show cow food and people food. People cannot digest grass. Sort pictures.
misconceptions.feedback: Some plants are food for animals but not for people. Grass is not food for us.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks every green leafy plant is a vegetable we can eat.

example.question: Is every green leafy plant a vegetable?
example.correct_answer: No, only some, like sukuma and spinach

misconceptions.cause: Vegetables at home are mostly green leaves.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, green leaves are vegetables" beside "No, only some, like sukuma and spinach" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Put sukuma, spinach and a weed side by side. Only some leaves are food.
misconceptions.feedback: Only some green leaves are vegetables. Ask an adult which ones.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks if a plant is edible, all its parts can be eaten.

example.question: We eat cassava roots. Can we eat cassava leaves raw and the stem?
example.correct_answer: No, we eat the roots (cooked); the stem is not food

misconceptions.cause: The child calls the whole plant "food".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, every part is food" beside "No, we eat the roots (cooked); the stem is not food" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Draw a maize plant: we eat the grains, not the stalk. A mango: the fruit, not the seed or bark.
misconceptions.feedback: We often eat only one part of a plant, like maize grains or mango fruit.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks flowers are edible because some plants we eat have flowers.

example.question: Is a rose flower food?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, flowers are part of plants we eat
example.correct_answer: No, roses are grown for beauty, not food

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes "plant" with "food plant".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, flowers are part of plants we eat" beside "No, roses are grown for beauty, not food" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Sort a basket: food plants and plants for beauty or timber.
misconceptions.feedback: Some plants are grown for beauty or wood, not for food.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: share ideas on types of animals found in the community,
talk about the uses of domestic animals to people,
talk about animals as cart pullers on the roads,
listen to a resource person, or read age appropriate stories on how to care for domestic animals,
role play care for domestic animals,
sing songs about the importance of animals to human beings.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you care for animals at home or school?
sub_strands.core_competences: Learning to Learn: learner develops the skill of working independently when role-playing care for domestic animals.
sub_strands.values: Love: learner enhances compassion when role playing care for domestic animals.
sub_strands.pcis: Socio-economic and Environmental Issues: learner promotes animal welfare education when advocating for the care of animals including those that provide animal power.
sub_strands.links: Care of animals can be used by learners when learning about creation in Religious Activities.

outcomes.text: explain the importance of domestic animals to human beings
determine ways of caring for domestic animals
engage in activities that care for domestic animals
reflect on the value of domestic animals to human beings

skills.name: Explain the importance of domestic animals and determine ways of caring for them
skills.mastery: Explains why domestic animals matter (milk, meat, eggs, skins and wool, manure, ploughing and carrying loads by oxen and donkeys, guarding by dogs, catching rats by cats, money from selling) and names ways of caring for them: food, clean water, a clean dry shelter, treating them when sick (by a vet), not beating or overloading them. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G3.RUBRIC.3.1), never as a phone question: c) engage in activities that care for domestic animals.
question_forms: which is cruel and which is caring

prerequisites.reason: Caring for animals in the locality, practised in Grade 2. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Relating food items to the animals that give them. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks domestic animals are kept only for food.

example.question: Why do some families keep a donkey?
example.correct_answer: To carry water and loads

misconceptions.cause: Animals at home are often talked about as milk, eggs and meat.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "To eat it" beside "To carry water and loads" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Make a chart of animals and their uses: donkey carries, dog guards, cat catches rats, ox ploughs.
misconceptions.feedback: Domestic animals help us in many ways: carrying, ploughing, guarding, and giving food.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks beating a donkey or ox makes it work better and is part of caring.

example.question: A donkey stops because its load is too heavy. What should be done?
example.correct_answer: Remove some of the load and let it rest

misconceptions.cause: Children see animals beaten on roads and copy what adults do.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Beat it so it moves" beside "Remove some of the load and let it rest" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Discuss how the animal feels. Fair treatment: right load, rest, water.
misconceptions.feedback: Beating an animal hurts it. Give it a load it can carry, rest and water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks animals get enough water from rain and wet grass, so they need not be watered.

example.question: Does a cow need to be given water every day?
example.correct_answer: Yes, every day

misconceptions.cause: Animals graze outside, so their needs seem met by nature.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, it drinks rain" beside "Yes, every day" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Compare with people: we drink every day. Show a water trough.
misconceptions.feedback: Animals need clean water every day, just like people.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a sick animal will get better by itself and does not need a vet.

example.question: A goat stops eating and looks weak. What should the family do?
example.correct_answer: Call a vet or animal health worker

misconceptions.cause: Small illnesses in people get better with rest, so the child expects the same.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wait, it will get better" beside "Call a vet or animal health worker" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Name the vet as the doctor for animals. A sick animal can die or spread disease.
misconceptions.feedback: A sick animal needs a vet, like a sick person needs a doctor.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: use pictures, video clips or realia to explore various types of waste materials in the environment,
discuss various ways of using waste to generate income in the immediate environment,
use digital devices or print materials to search for more information on ways of making money from waste,
discuss safety measures to be observed when handling waste materials,
undertake activities that can manage waste materials in the environment using unique and new ideas,
undertake a project that will put waste materials from the environment into appropriate use,
display transparency when accounting for money generated from the project.
key_inquiry_questions: How can waste materials be used to generate income?
sub_strands.core_competences: Creativity and Imagination: learner develops unique and new ideas when undertaking activities that can manage waste materials in the environment.
sub_strands.values: Integrity: learner enhances accountability in displaying transparency when accounting for money generated from the projects.
sub_strands.pcis: Health promotion issues: learner develops habits of safety and hygiene when handling waste materials.
sub_strands.links: Income generation from items made from waste materials is related to concepts of measurement (money) in Mathematical Activities.

outcomes.text: identify waste materials that can be used to generate income
describe ways in which waste materials can generate income
carry out activities to manage waste materials in the environment
value the use of different waste materials to make money in the community

skills.name: Identify waste materials that can generate income and describe how
skills.mastery: Names waste that can bring money (plastic bottles, scrap metal, paper and cartons, tins, old tyres, glass bottles collected by an adult, kitchen waste for compost, banana fibres, old clothes) and describes how: selling to collectors and recyclers, making items to sell (mats, baskets, toys, tyre sandals, paper bags), making manure to sell; knows sharp, broken or medical waste is never picked by children. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G3.RUBRIC.3.1), never as a phone question: c) carry out activities to manage waste materials in the environment.

prerequisites.reason: Keeping the school clean: collecting and sorting litter. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Needs, wants and money: the start of financial literacy. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks all waste is useless rubbish that can only be burnt or thrown away.

example.question: Can an empty plastic bottle earn money?
example.correct_answer: Yes, it can be sold to a recycler or made into something

misconceptions.cause: At home waste goes straight into the pit or fire.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, it is rubbish" beside "Yes, it can be sold to a recycler or made into something" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show items made from waste (a bottle-top toy, a tyre sandal) and a collector buying plastics.
misconceptions.feedback: Many waste materials can earn money if we sell them or make things from them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks children can pick any waste to sell, including broken glass and syringes.

example.question: You see a used syringe on the dumping site. What do you do?
example.correct_answer: Do not touch it; tell an adult

misconceptions.cause: If waste is worth money, all of it seems worth collecting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Pick it and sell it" beside "Do not touch it; tell an adult" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a "never touch" list: broken glass, syringes, sharp tins, medical waste. Tell an adult.
misconceptions.feedback: Never touch broken glass, syringes or sharp waste. Tell an adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks burning plastic is the best way to manage waste because it disappears.

example.question: What is a better way to deal with plastic bottles than burning them?
example.correct_answer: Collect and sell them to a recycler, or reuse them

misconceptions.cause: Burning removes waste from sight quickly.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Burning, it makes them disappear" beside "Collect and sell them to a recycler, or reuse them" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show the black smoke from burning plastic in a picture. Say it harms the lungs and air.
misconceptions.feedback: Burning plastic makes harmful smoke. Collect, reuse or sell it instead.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks kitchen peels have no use and cannot earn anything.

example.question: What can banana and potato peels be used for?
example.correct_answer: To make compost manure for the garden or to sell

misconceptions.cause: Peels smell and rot, so they seem worthless.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing" beside "To make compost manure for the garden or to sell" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Start a small compost heap at school. Show the manure after some weeks.
misconceptions.feedback: Peels can be turned into compost manure that helps plants grow and can be sold.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.
